newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli GDP will grow 3.7 pct in 1997 - Hapoalim.
newsitem.headline: Israeli GDP will grow 3.7 pct in 1997 - Hapoalim.

text.p: Bank Hapoalim said on Monday that Israel's gross domestic product would grow 3.7 percent this year, up from the 3.2 percent it previously forecasted.

In its quarterly economic survey, the bank did not say exactly why it revised its forecast upward, but it did note that one other key indicator it was upgrading was merchandise exports. It said they would grow 8.0 percent this year, rather than its 5.0 percent earlier estimate.

Hapoalim's forecast compares with a 4.4 percent increase in gross domestic product growth 1996, according to preliminary estimates by the Central Bureau of Statistics. The Treasury is forecasting a four percent expansion this year.

The bank said the engines of Israel's previous fast-paced expansion -- the wave of immigration, the economic stability programme, the peace process and high technology -- continued to have a positive influence on the economy.

Hapoalim said the higher forecasted export growth was due to an improved exchange rate environment. It said it now expects the Israeli shekel to depreciate seven percent over the year against the basket of foreign currencies compared with its earlier estimate of six percent.

A Hapoalim source said the revised estimate of the shekel's depreciation was made before the turmoil in the domestic forex market in the second half of January and might be subject to further revision later on.
The shekel has been trading at the bottom of its official trading band forcing the central bank to intervene heavily in the currency market.

Hapolaim also revised upward its forecast for growth in civilian merchandise imports to 6.2 percent from 4.7 percent. Nevertheless, the bank said it expected the current account deficit to narrow to $4.4 billion from an earlier estimate of $5.0 billion and an estimated $4.6 billion in 1996.
The bank revised downward its forecasted growth of investment in fixed assets to 2.0 percent from 3.2 this year.
Israel's consumer price index will rise 8.5 percent for the year, down from an earlier estimate of 9.0 percent and a 10.6 percent rate in 1996, Hapoalim said.
